config.title: Observability at scale

intro.title: Observability at scale
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple, scalable observability dashboard that visualizes simulated system metrics like CPU usage and request latency. You'll learn the core concept of instrumenting code to collect and aggregate telemetry data, which is essential for monitoring large-scale systems. The main technologies involved include metric collection libraries, time-series databases, and basic visualization tools. By the end, you'll understand how to implement observability patterns that help detect and diagnose issues in production environments.
intro.usecase: In production engineering, observability at scale is the backbone of monitoring large, distributed systems like e-commerce platforms or cloud services. Engineers use centralized dashboards to visualize real-time metrics—such as latency, error rates, and resource utilization—across thousands of servers. This enables rapid detection of anomalies, like a sudden spike in API errors during a flash sale, allowing teams to diagnose and resolve issues before they impact users. Implementing this pattern ensures system reliability and performance at massive scale.

objectives: Implement a centralized logging system to aggregate application events
Configure distributed tracing to monitor request flows across microservices
Construct a metrics collection pipeline for system performance monitoring
Initialize alerting rules based on predefined thresholds and anomaly detection
Integrate observability tools with existing infrastructure components
Manipulate sampling rates to balance observability data volume with system overhead
Render dashboards that visualize key performance indicators and system health

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package to enable component state management for observability at scale.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and hooks
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: React and useState are imported, ready for building observable components.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported React and useState, which are essential for managing state in React components—a foundational skill for building observable systems at scale.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported React, but remember to also import useState from 'react' to manage component state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. For this lesson, you need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the ObservabilityDashboard component
steps.instruction: Create a functional React component named ObservabilityDashboard that returns a div container.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function with the name ObservabilityDashboard that returns a JSX div element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the ObservabilityDashboard component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a functional component named ObservabilityDashboard that returns a div container.
successCriteria: A component named ObservabilityDashboard is defined and returns a JSX div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main component structure for the observability dashboard.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the component is named exactly 'ObservabilityDashboard' and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've named it 'ObservabilityDashboard' and it returns a div.

steps.title: Initialize service health state
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'serviceHealth' initialized as an empty array.
steps.hint: Call useState with [] as the initial value and destructure the returned array into a variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state with an empty array
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a serviceHealth state variable ready to store service health data.
successCriteria: The component contains a useState call that initializes serviceHealth as an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've initialized the serviceHealth state variable. This will allow us to track the health status of monitored services.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with [] as the initial value and naming the variable 'serviceHealth'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to use useState to create a state variable called 'serviceHealth' initialized as an empty array inside the component.

steps.title: Initialize metrics data state
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, use useState to create a state variable named 'metricsData' initialized as an empty array.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call after your existing serviceHealth state. The initial value should be an empty array [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing array state
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: serviceHealth for service status and metricsData for storing collected metrics.
successCriteria: The component contains a 'metricsData' state variable initialized as an empty array using useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the metricsData state. This will store the collected metrics data for observability monitoring.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'metricsData' with an initial value of an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: The metricsData state isn't properly initialized. You need to add a useState call that creates a 'metricsData' variable initialized as an empty array.

steps.title: Define loadHealthData handler
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, define a function named loadHealthData that simulates loading service health data by updating the serviceHealth state with a sample value.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses setServiceHealth to change the serviceHealth state to a sample value like 'degraded' or 'unhealthy'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A loadHealthData function is defined that updates serviceHealth state when called.
successCriteria: The component contains a function named loadHealthData that calls setServiceHealth with a sample health value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a handler that simulates loading health data, which is essential for observability at scale.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named loadHealthData and updates the serviceHealth state using setServiceHealth.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loadHealthData function isn't defined correctly. It should update the serviceHealth state with a sample value.

steps.title: Define loadMetricsData handler
steps.instruction: Define a function named loadMetricsData inside your ObservabilityDashboard component that simulates loading metrics data. This function should update the metricsData state with sample metrics.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setMetricsData with an object containing sample metrics like responseTime, errorRate, and throughput.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a loadMetricsData function that updates the metricsData state with sample metrics data.
successCriteria: The component contains a function named loadMetricsData that calls setMetricsData with an object containing sample metrics properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the loadMetricsData handler that simulates loading metrics data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it updates the metricsData state with sample metrics using setMetricsData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loadMetricsData function is missing or doesn't properly update the metricsData state.

steps.title: Add dashboard header and title
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component's return statement, add a header section with an h1 element containing the title 'Observability Dashboard'.
steps.hint: Add a <header> element with an <h1> inside it. Place this before the existing return null; statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The dashboard now has a visible header with the title 'Observability Dashboard' displayed in an h1 element.
successCriteria: The component returns a header element containing an h1 with the exact text 'Observability Dashboard'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the dashboard header with the proper title. This establishes the basic structure for your observability dashboard.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both the header element and the h1 with the exact title text 'Observability Dashboard'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The header structure isn't quite right. Remember to add a header element containing an h1 with the text 'Observability Dashboard'.

steps.title: Add metrics section and display data
steps.instruction: Add a metrics section to your ObservabilityDashboard component with a heading and map through the metricsData state to display each metric's key-value pair.
steps.hint: Create a <section> element with an <h2> heading for 'Metrics'. Inside, use Object.entries(metricsData).map() to iterate over the metrics and render each one.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new section with a 'Metrics' heading appears in the dashboard, ready to display key-value pairs from the metricsData state.
successCriteria: The component includes a <section> element with an <h2> heading for 'Metrics' and uses Object.entries(metricsData).map() to render each metric.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the metrics section to the dashboard. This allows you to display key observability metrics at scale.

steps.feedbackWrong: The metrics section is not properly added. Ensure you have a <section> with an <h2> heading and use Object.entries(metricsData).map() to iterate through the metrics.

steps.title: Add load data buttons and wire handlers
steps.instruction: Inside the ObservabilityDashboard component's return statement, add two buttons: one with the text 'Load Health Data' that calls the loadHealthData handler when clicked, and another with the text 'Load Metrics Data' that calls the loadMetricsData handler when clicked.
steps.hint: Place the buttons after the existing header and before the service health section. Use the onClick attribute to wire each button to its corresponding handler function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The dashboard will have two interactive buttons that trigger data loading functions when clicked, enabling users to simulate loading observability data.
successCriteria: Two buttons are added with the correct text labels and onClick handlers wired to loadHealthData and loadMetricsData functions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added interactive buttons to load observability data, which is essential for simulating real-time monitoring in production systems.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but check that both buttons have the correct text labels and are properly wired to their respective handler functions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or not correctly implemented. Make sure to add two buttons with 'Load Health Data' and 'Load Metrics Data' text, each with onClick handlers calling the corresponding functions.
